Resonance.role: Important people, conditions, consequences, and changes have a way of reaching attention.

Coherence.plain_question: Are the important parts working together?
Coherence.role: What matters, what is decided, and what is done can reinforce rather than undermine one another.

Correspondence.plain_question: Are we seeing things as they really are?
Correspondence.role: Understanding and decisions remain answerable to what conditions and consequences are showing.

Correctability.plain_question: When something is not working, can we actually change course?
Correctability.role: Divergence can lead to meaningful adjustment and renewed contact.

HighBalanced.summary: All four capacities are reported as consistently available and relatively even. This does not mean the person or group will remain oriented under every pressure. The useful inquiry is what makes this pattern possible and how those conditions can be sustained when circumstances change.

Balanced.summary: The four capacities sit relatively close together. There is no strong evidence that one part alone is interrupting the process. Look at the conditions surrounding the whole pattern, and identify situations where the complete sequence works especially well.

LowBalanced.summary: All four capacities are reported as difficult to access consistently. This is not evidence that the person or group lacks them. Begin with a real exception: a moment when attention, shared understanding, reality-checking, and adjustment worked better. What was different then?

Uneven.summary: Some capacities are much more available than others. The strongest capacity is a resource, and the gap is an invitation to understand what happens between the two—not proof that one capacity causes the other to falter.

R_P.headline: We may be noticing more than we are making sense of.
R_P.individual: Important signals may be reaching your attention, but the harder task may be deciding what they mean and checking your first interpretation. More information alone may not create clarity. It may help to slow down, sort what you have noticed, and ask which parts are evidence and which are assumptions.
R_P.collective: The group may be hearing concerns, perspectives, and changes without turning them into a shared understanding. The issue may not be a lack of voices; it may be what happens after they are heard. How does the group compare perspectives, test its first reading, and decide what deserves attention?
R_P.so_what_individual: When signals arrive faster than they can be understood, you may react to the loudest or newest thing rather than the most important one. That can make priorities shift repeatedly and leave important consequences unexplored.
R_P.so_what_collective: When signals enter but are not brought into shared understanding, different people may act on different versions of what is happening. Meetings can produce more information without producing a clearer common picture.
R_P.doorway_individual: Find a recent moment when you noticed something important and made sense of it well. What helped you separate the signal from your first assumption? What would help you use that approach in a more difficult situation?
R_P.doorway_collective: Find a recent moment when the group heard a difficult or unexpected signal and reached a useful shared understanding. Who helped make that possible? What process allowed differing perspectives to be heard and tested?

C_P.headline: We may be working from a shared picture that needs testing.
C_P.individual: Your priorities may fit together reasonably well, yet the picture that holds them together may not fully match current conditions. Being consistent can feel reassuring. The important question is whether your assumptions are still accurate as circumstances change.
C_P.collective: The group may have clear shared priorities and internal agreement while some common assumptions remain insufficiently tested. Agreement helps people coordinate, but agreement alone cannot show whether the shared picture is accurate.
C_P.so_what_individual: A person can make consistent choices and still move confidently in the wrong direction if the assumptions behind those choices are outdated. The risk is not a lack of commitment; it is commitment built around a picture that has stopped matching reality.
C_P.so_what_collective: An organization can coordinate efficiently around a mistaken assumption. The more aligned its people become around that assumption, the harder it may be for contrary evidence to change the shared direction.
C_P.doorway_individual: Choose one important belief guiding your current priorities. What recent experience supports it? What challenges it? What would you expect to see if the belief were no longer accurate?
C_P.doorway_collective: Identify one assumption that shapes an important group priority. Whose experience could test it? What evidence would cause the group to revise its shared view?

P_K.headline: We may see what is happening but struggle to change what we do.
P_K.individual: You may be reasonably good at testing assumptions and recognizing when something is not working. The harder part may come afterwards: turning what you see into a different response. More analysis may not be the next step if the problem is already understood.
P_K.collective: The group may recognize when its assumptions or decisions do not match reality, yet struggle to turn that recognition into action. The missing link may involve decision authority, competing incentives, coordination, trust, resources, or the cost of changing course. The assessment cannot determine which; it identifies where to investigate.
P_K.so_what_individual: When recognition does not lead to a different response, the same problem can return even though you understand it. This can create frustration and reduce confidence in your own ability to act on what you know.
P_K.so_what_collective: When a group repeatedly acknowledges a problem without changing practice, people may learn that speaking honestly has little effect. Over time, discussion and action become detached, and the same consequences recur.
P_K.doorway_individual: Recall a time you changed course after realizing something was not working. What made action possible then—permission, support, a smaller first step, a clear choice, or something else? What of that condition is available now?
P_K.doorway_collective: Find an example when the group turned an uncomfortable finding into a real change. What enabled that movement—authority, trust, resources, agreement, or timing? Which of those conditions is missing in the current situation?

K_C.headline: We may be able to adjust, but lose sight of what should hold the parts together.
K_C.individual: You may be able to respond when something goes wrong, while the priorities guiding those responses compete with one another. The question is whether each adjustment moves you toward what matters or simply deals with the latest demand.
K_C.collective: The group may respond quickly to problems while its priorities or functions remain poorly connected. Repeated adjustments can keep activity moving without resolving the tensions that make the same problems return.
K_C.so_what_individual: If each response is made separately, you may spend energy correcting one issue only to create strain somewhere else. A clearer sense of what matters most can help you decide which changes belong together.
K_C.so_what_collective: An organization can become very good at firefighting while remaining unclear about shared direction. One team’s fix may create another team’s problem, and repeated corrections consume attention that could be used to address the underlying tension.
K_C.doorway_individual: Look at two recent adjustments you made. Did they support the same priority, or pull you in different directions? What principle could help you decide which changes belong together?
K_C.doorway_collective: Choose a recurring issue that crosses team or functional boundaries. Where does one unit’s correction create a problem for another? What shared outcome could help the parts coordinate their adjustments?

R_C.headline: We may notice what is happening but struggle to connect it with what matters.
R_C.individual: You may be alert to changes and signals, yet competing priorities can make it hard to decide what they mean for your choices. Noticing more is not always the answer; the next step may be connecting what you already see to what matters most.
R_C.collective: The group may hear important signals, but those signals can remain separated across roles, teams, or priorities. People may each understand part of the situation without being able to bring those parts into a common direction.
R_C.so_what_individual: Without a way to connect new information to your priorities, attention can become scattered. You may know that many things matter but find it difficult to decide what deserves a response first.
R_C.so_what_collective: When signals remain inside separate functions, the organization may respond in fragments. Important relationships between issues are missed, and decisions can solve local problems while weakening the whole.
R_C.doorway_individual: Choose a recent signal that caught your attention. Which of your priorities did it affect? What helped—or prevented—you from deciding what it meant for your next choice?
R_C.doorway_collective: Take a recent issue that touched more than one part of the group. Where did each part see something different? What conversation would help connect those views to a shared decision?

P_R.headline: We may test our conclusions carefully—but are we noticing the right things?
P_R.individual: You may be careful about checking assumptions and weighing evidence. Yet careful reasoning can only work with what reaches your attention. Important experiences, changes, or consequences may still be missing from the picture you are testing.
P_R.collective: The group may examine the information it has with care while hearing from a limited range of people or experiences. A well-run review can still miss what never entered the room or the data being considered.
P_R.so_what_individual: You can reach a sound conclusion from incomplete information and still misunderstand the situation. Before refining the analysis, it may be worth asking what or whom you have not considered.
P_R.so_what_collective: The group may make defensible decisions based on an incomplete field of information. People closest to an effect, quieter voices, or early signs of change may be absent from the shared picture.
P_R.doorway_individual: Think of a decision you felt confident about. Whose perspective or what consequence did you not consider at first? What helped you notice it later?
P_R.doorway_collective: Identify whose experience is least likely to enter the group's decisions. How could that perspective be heard early enough to change the shared understanding rather than merely validate a decision already made?

Resonance.individual: Where are you already noticing something important that you once overlooked, and what made that possible?
Resonance.collective: Where does the group already hear signals it might previously have missed, and what conditions make those signals safe and possible to bring forward?

Coherence.individual: Where do your priorities already reinforce one another, and what is different when they begin to compete?
Coherence.collective: Where do different parts of the group already work together well, and what conditions allow that alignment to hold?

Correspondence.individual: Where have you recently changed your mind because reality showed you something different, and what made that revision possible?
Correspondence.collective: Where has the group recently revised an assumption because conditions or consequences showed something different, and what made that possible?

Correctability.individual: Where have you genuinely changed course after recognizing something was not working, and what enabled the change?
Correctability.collective: Where has the group turned recognition into meaningful change, and what authority, trust, or conditions enabled that movement?

individual_sequence: specific everyday consequence and why it matters
appreciative doorway grounded in the strongest reported capacity or a concrete exception
collective_sequence: organizational consequences and possible structural conditions without causal assertion
collective inquiry grounded in a working example or enabling condition
composition_contract.overall_indicator: Show the arithmetic average and its public band as a secondary descriptor. Do not use it to override the four-dimensional pattern.
composition_contract.selection: Use first qualifying relationship in the canonical precedence order; include profile shape as context; use strongest and lowest capacities as supporting evidence.
composition_contract.anti_genericity: A generated synthesis must name at least two actual dimension scores and explain their relationship. If no relationship threshold qualifies, use the balanced/shape narrative and strongest/lowest capacity context.
composition_contract.forbidden: diagnostic labels, rankings, causal claims not supported by responses, generic paragraph repeated regardless of score vector

score_profile_selector.manual_full_report_variants: not authored individually; profile synthesis is assembled from explicit components
score_profile_selector.interpretation_caveat: A score pattern identifies where inquiry may be useful; it does not establish cause.
